description: Ground Truth talks from BSides Las Vegas 2026.

talks.title: Wednesday
talks.teaser: Covers anomaly detection for surfacing rare attacks, AI agents in defense competitions, and social engineering bots.
talks.summary:
This recording is a block of three back-to-back talks. The first, from Sophos data scientists, looks at why security detectors fail on rare behavior that labeled training data never covers. The team ran isolation forest, k-means distance and PCA reconstruction error over unlabeled command-line and file data to pick the most unusual samples, had a large language model label them, and retrained the detectors. On a harder test set, the command-line detector's ROC AUC rose from about 0.6 to about 0.9. The same approach carried over to RTF and HTML classifiers, using a dual-prompt method where two opposing judges had to agree before a label was kept. No single anomaly method won on every dataset.

The second talk reports on AI agents used by students in cyber defense and incident response competitions, with all teams given the same logged, audited access. Most teams used agents like search engines and gave thin context, while red teams that had prepared agent frameworks did better. Defending cost far more than attacking, and AI-written incident reports contained confident fabrications. The takeaways were to supply context up front, validate outputs, and authorize actions in advance.

The third talk, by Kora Gortney, frames social engineering as a set of influence patterns such as urgency, authority and reciprocity, and tests them against two chatbots in the audience. A bot with an added knowledge base did not reliably refuse more often than a plain baseline, so explicit knowledge alone did not change results much. The talk argues that detecting these patterns with tooling could reduce the load on people.

talks.title: Tuesday
talks.teaser: Surveys social engineering research, from cognitive attack models to AI-driven scams and LLM context poisoning.
talks.summary:
This Ground Truth stage block bundles several back-to-back talks on how people and AI systems get manipulated. The opening talk frames attackers through a cognitive attack taxonomy that links vulnerabilities, exploits and tactics, and argues that the surrounding environment shapes what an attacker can do. A second talk treats employees as differentiated groups rather than one uniform role, drawing on telemetry about AI tool enablement and executive behavior to show that some populations carry more risk than others.

Later sessions move into AI systems. One presentation shows how a single planted document can flip an LLM's decision, with extra supporting documents adding little and stronger models resisting more often. The speakers test defenses such as trust tags, prompt guardrails and a structured voting step that keeps the model out of the final decision. Other talks analyze recorded vishing calls to find recurring sequences of authority, victim framing and transfer requests, and report a large benchmark of AI-enabled scams that measures persuasion success and cost per scam.

The practical takeaways are to treat untrusted content as a constant attack vector, separate fuzzy LLM reasoning from deterministic decision logic, and tailor awareness and controls to specific cohorts. Several findings are preliminary and rest on small or synthetic samples, so the presenters frame them as directional rather than conclusive.

talks.title: Monday
talks.teaser: Collects several Ground Truth talks on AI-driven scams, vulnerability prioritization, prompt security and agent hacking.
talks.summary:
This recording of the Ground Truth track's Monday block strings together several separate talks rather than one presentation. It opens with voice phishing: a large survey experiment compares AI voice models with human scam callers. The findings suggest that message content matters more than how human a voice sounds, and that some automated calls already look profitable, though they cost more per minute than email.

The middle sessions cover trust-based scams, where a system uses AI personas to engage inbound scammers and map conversation stages before a payment request. Another talk examines exploitation timing and the EPSS scoring model, arguing that prioritizing by probability works better than severity scores. A further session presents a BERT-based classifier that separates harmful goals from the framing used to disguise them.

The final talks address a vulnerability pipeline that silently drops findings when joins fail, and a study of AI agents attempting CTF challenges. The first shows how left joins, fallback matching and evidence packets keep unowned assets visible. The second finds that agents often succeed through pattern matching, and that open-weight models trail closed ones by less than expected at far lower cost.
